questions.q: What is the real reason ServiceNow uses one base table, `cmdb_ci`, instead of a separate unrelated table per CI type?
options: A shared base table lets common fields and cross-CI relationships work uniformly across every CI type
ServiceNow only allows a maximum of one table per application
Separate tables would be faster to query
There is no real benefit; it's purely historical
questions.explain: A shared base table means a relationship or report can reference "any CI" generically, and every subclass automatically inherits the same core fields with the same names.

questions.q: Which fields does `cmdb_ci_server` add that the generic base `cmdb_ci` table doesn't need?
options: CPU count, RAM, disk capacity, and operating system
questions.explain: CPU, RAM, disk, and OS are server-specific attributes a generic CI, a network switch, or a database wouldn't need.

questions.q: Why would putting CPU and RAM fields directly on the base `cmdb_ci` table be a real problem, not just untidy?
options: It would make the table extension mechanism stop working entirely
Every CI, including switches and services that will never use those fields, would carry them unused
ServiceNow would refuse to save any CI record
It would delete the existing subclasses
questions.explain: Every subclass inherits whatever lives on the base table, so fields relevant only to servers would sit empty and unused on every non-server CI.

questions.q: Which CI subclass is only previewed in this chapter, with full depth saved for Chapter 3's CSDM content?
questions.explain: cmdb_ci_service represents business and technical services, which get full treatment once CSDM's domains are introduced in Chapter 3.

questions.q: The `cmdb_ci` table hierarchy uses the exact same extension pattern you already learned on which other base table?
questions.explain: Platform Fundamentals taught table extension on `task` — Incident, Problem, and Change all extend it the same way CI subclasses extend `cmdb_ci`.
